question: Explain the increase in boiling points of the alkanes, as indicated in the table.
memo: • Structure: The chain length / molecular size / molecular structure / molecular mass / surface area increases. $\checkmark$\n• Intermolecular forces: Increase in strength of intermolecular forces / induced dipole / London / dispersion / Van der Waals forces / momentary dipoles. $\checkmark$\n• Energy: More energy needed to overcome/break intermolecular forces. $\checkmark$
final_answer: Chain length and molecular mass increase, leading to stronger intermolecular forces (London forces) which require more energy to overcome.

question: Explain the difference between the boiling points of an alkane and an alcohol, each having THREE carbon atoms per molecule, by referring to the TYPE of intermolecular forces.
memo:
• Alkanes have London / dispersion / induced dipole forces. $\checkmark$
• Alcohols have hydrogen bonding (in addition to London / dispersion / induced dipole forces and dipole-dipole forces). $\checkmark$
• Hydrogen bonding are stronger intermolecular forces than London / dispersion / induced dipole forces. $\checkmark$
• Alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes. $\checkmark$
final_answer: Alkanes have London forces, while alcohols have hydrogen bonding, which are stronger intermolecular forces requiring more energy to break.

question: Refer to the relative strengths of oxidising agents to explain which ONE of the two ions will preferably be involved in the plating process.
memo: $\text{Ag}^+$ / silver(I) ions is a stronger oxidising agent $\checkmark$ than $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ / Copper(II) ions and will be reduced (more readily) $\checkmark$ to form silver/Ag on the iron rod.
final_answer: $\text{Ag}^+$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and will be reduced more readily.
